_readme: Mission Control Live script (P3 owns the words, P1 runs scripts/narrate.py). CAPCOM = the rookie's boss: professional, dry, teaches the science, and now and then roasts the rookie (funny, never mean-spirited). INTERN = a timid but dedicated rookie: soft-spoken, stammers, takes notes and genuinely wants to do the job well, even though everything in space scares him. Never stupid, just easily rattled. Still PANICS (genuinely, screaming) when the risk score is over 90, is nervous in between, and is RELIEVED when it's low. CAPCOM always has the last word on the honest science. Words in [square brackets] are ElevenLabs v4 delivery tags (e.g. [panicking]); they are acted, never spoken, and the subtitles hide them. Keep each line under ~12 seconds out loud.

intern_tones._readme: The INTERN's delivery follows the risk score (web/api/script.js BANDS) or the line's tag (dialogue.js toneOf). Lower stability + higher style = more dramatic.

intro: Mission Control, live. Forty-two thousand near-Earth asteroids on the board.
[gasps] Forty-two THOUSAND? Are they all coming HERE?
No. That's why we built a model to tell us which ones deserve worry. Sit down, rookie.
welcome: Welcome, Intern. Glad you could make it. Hope you're ready to get started. Your job: watch the asteroids near Earth. Each one gets a risk score. High score, we watch it closer.
[nervous, eager] Watch the rocks, check the scores. Y-yes, sir. I won't let you down.
risk_on: Risk colors. Every dot is an asteroid, colored by the model's verdict.
Red means the model flags it as potentially hazardous: big enough, and its orbit passes close to Earth's. Blue means low risk.
[nervous] So red is... bad. Red is coming for us?
Red means keep watching it. Not that it's coming. The bigger the dot, the higher the score.
[timid, determined] Red, watch it. Blue, relax. Okay. I'm writing that down.
Good. You'll see a lot more blue than red. Try to stay conscious.
show_all_on: Until now you've been seeing one asteroid in five, so the screen stays readable. This is all of them. Over forty-two thousand.
[gasps, horrified] Forty-two THOUSAND?! That's... that's not a solar system, that's a snow globe!
Those are just the near-Earth ones we've found. Most will never come anywhere close to us.
[shaky] 'Just the ones we've found.' You said that so casually.
test_only: Unseen test set. About eighty-five hundred asteroids the model never saw while it was training.
[nervous] Like a pop quiz? I'm, um... not great at pop quizzes.
It's how you find out if the model actually learned the physics or just memorized the answers.
results: The report card. Recall: how many real hazards we caught. Precision: how many of our alarms were real.
[earnest] Recall, caught. Precision, real. Got it. Can I... can I keep a copy of this?
act1: First, we gave the model everything.
Even the closest-approach distance. It rediscovered NASA's exact rule for hazardous asteroids. Nobody told it.
[impressed] Huh. It learned that faster than me.
A houseplant learns faster than you.
act2: Model B. We took away the answer key: no closest-approach distance.
[nervous] So it's... guessing? Like I do?
No. It works out the geometry from the shape of the orbit. You guess.
mistakes: Mistakes mode. Magenta: real hazards the model missed. Yellow: false alarms, safe rocks it flagged anyway.
[horrified] It makes MISTAKES? It MISSED some?
Every model does. Ours shows you where. Missing a hazard is worse than a false alarm, so magenta is the one to study.
[timid] Okay. Magenta first. I'll study magenta.
act4: Hidden hazards. Here's the part nobody expected. NASA judges an asteroid's size by how bright it looks.
[timid] That... makes sense? Big rock, bright rock?
Unless it's dark. So we went looking for big, dark rocks near Earth's orbit that the brightness rule calls small.
{hidden_measured}. The lime-green ones. Each measured by NASA's own telescope at a hundred and forty meters or more. None on the hazard list.
[panicking] Oh no. Oh no no no. Should I call NASA? I should call NASA. I'll be polite about it!
They're candidates for a second look, not incoming. And no. You do not call NASA.
custom: Design your own asteroid. The model will judge it live.
[nervous] Please don't make a big one. Please don't make a big one.

near_miss_start: [panicking, breathing fast] Oh no no no, WAIT, wait wait wait...
near_miss_end_1: It missed. By millions of kilometers.
near_miss_end_2: Relax. That's a near miss in space terms. Still millions of kilometers.
custom_hit: [whimpering] Can we undo that? Is there an undo button?
custom_chill_1: [long sigh of relief] Oh, thank goodness. Boring. I LOVE boring.
custom_chill_2: That one's not coming anywhere near us.
[relieved laugh] Cancel the bunker. Cancel my will.
custom_sus_1: Hm. The model's a little nervous.
You get nervous when the printer beeps.
custom_screwed_1: [panicking] Oh no. Oh no no NO. Is it too late to quit?!
High risk score means keep watching it, not that it's coming. Breathe, rookie.
custom_screwed_2: [panicking, voice cracking] Why would you BUILD that?!
For science. It's a what-if. Put the fire extinguisher down.

report._react_readme: chill = under 20, sus = under Model B's cutoff (75), screwed = cutoff to 90, panic = over 90

chill: [long sigh of relief] Oh, thank goodness.
[relieved laugh] Phew. Boring. I love boring.
[exhales] Okay. Okay, good. My heart can start again.
sus: [nervous] Is that... bad? That sounds bad.
[uneasy] Should I be sitting down for this?
screwed: [nervous, voice shaking] That's... a big number. That's a really big number.
[anxious] Okay. I'm fine. I'm totally fine. Am I fine?
[nervous laugh] Ha... ha. Is that high? That feels high.
panic: [panicking, screaming] AAAH! No no no NO NO!
[panicking, breathing fast] Oh no. Oh no no no. Where's the bunker?! WHERE IS THE BUNKER?!
[screaming] It's RED! Why is it RED?!
[panicking] Is it too late to apply somewhere else?! Like, on a different PLANET?!

chill: Nothing to see here. Go back to your sandwich.
Safe. You can come out from under the desk now.
sus: Worth a second look. Not worth panicking. Which, for you, is a stretch.
Keep one eye on it. Use the other one to read the manual.
screwed: Hazardous means its orbit passes close enough to keep watching. Not that it's coming.
We're fine. You're the one I'm worried about.
panic: Rookie. Breathe. Look at the screen.
Red means watch it closely. It does not mean it's coming. Nobody here predicts impacts.
[shaky exhale] ...Okay. Okay. Watching. I can watch.
Good. Now take the trash can off your head.

nasa_disagrees: NASA. This one's our mistake. At least the model admits it. Take notes, rookie.

hidden: [long sigh of relief] Oh, thank goodness.
NASA judged it by brightness. But it's dark. It's about {size} meters of rock.
[panicking] Wait, that's big enough to COUNT! Why didn't anyone SAY so?!
We just did. It's a candidate for a second look, not a threat. Somebody should tell NASA. Not you.
whatif: Hypothetically. If {name} hit us at {speed} kilometers per second...
It is not going to hit. This is a what-if. Please stop screaming into the headset.

q+: its closest point to the Sun sits right around Earth's distance
it swings in to exactly where Earth lives
q-: its closest point to the Sun stays well away from Earth's orbit
it never comes in as close as we are
ad+: its whole orbit stays in Earth's neighborhood
it never wanders far from our part of space
ad-: it spends most of its time far out past Mars
its orbit swings way out, far from us
a+: its orbit is about the same size as Earth's
it laps the Sun on a track a lot like ours
a-: its orbit is a very different size from Earth's
its track around the Sun doesn't match ours
e+: its stretched-out orbit cuts across our path
its orbit is long enough to cross ours
e-: its orbit is too round to reach us
its orbit doesn't stretch far enough to meet ours
i+: it orbits almost flat, in the same plane as Earth
it travels in our lane, not above or below it
i-: its orbit is tilted steeply away from ours
it passes way above or below our lane
om+: its orbit happens to be turned toward our path
the way its orbit is turned lines it up with ours
om-: its orbit is turned away from our path
the way its orbit is turned keeps it out of our way
w+: its closest point to the Sun lines up with Earth's orbit
it crosses our plane right where Earth is
w-: it crosses our plane far from where Earth orbits
its orbit is pointed the wrong way to meet ours

radio.text: Short NASA mission control radio squelch and static beep, quindar tone

alarm.text: Spaceship control room warning alarm, two urgent beeps

whoosh.text: Fast deep whoosh of a large rock flying past, cinematic

impact.text: Massive asteroid impact explosion, deep rumbling boom with long debris rumble
